II / Onboarding Flow

From sign-up to first generated item — 7 steps, under 15 minutes

Onboarding for faculty is different from students. Faculty come in with existing materials and existing courses. The goal is to get them to their first generated item as fast as possible — ideally within the same session they sign up. The onboarding wizard should never feel like a gate; it should feel like a shortcut.

Onboarding wizard — 7 steps

1
Account setup — name, specialty, institution
First name, last name, MSM email (verified via SAML/SSO or magic link). Specialty dropdown (pre-populated from UMLS semantic types: Cardiology, Pharmacology, Pathology, etc.). Role: Course Director, Lecturer, or Teaching Faculty. This data configures the default USMLE topic filters and generation defaults.
2
Upload your first document — syllabus or lecture
Full-page drag-and-drop area. Accepts PPTX, PDF, DOCX. Two labeled zones: "Syllabus" (creates a course structure) and "Lecture" (creates content for generation). Copy: "Start with a syllabus to create your course in one step, or upload a lecture to jump straight to questions." Minimum: one file to proceed.
3
Watch processing — transparent pipeline with real-time steps
Full-screen processing animation. Shows each pipeline step as it completes: Extracting text → Chunking → Embedding → UMLS enrichment → Building concept graph → Ready. Small explanatory sentence under each step ("We're linking your content to 3.4M medical concepts"). Not a spinner — actual progress with meaning. Faculty learn what the system does while they wait.
4
Review extracted concepts — first look at the knowledge graph
Shows top 15-20 extracted SubConcepts with UMLS links and evidence grades. Faculty can approve, merge duplicates, or flag incorrect extractions. This is the first "wow moment" — seeing their lecture content transformed into a structured knowledge map. Action: "These look right, continue" or "Let me clean these up." Brief copy explaining that better-reviewed concepts = better questions.
5
Create or confirm your course — one click if syllabus was uploaded
If a syllabus was uploaded: system proposes a course name (extracted from document), course code (MEDI-601 format), and week structure. Faculty confirm or edit. If lecture only: fill in course name and code manually. This step takes 30 seconds when a syllabus is present. Creates the CatalogCourse + first Block + first section.
6
Generate your first 5 questions — instant gratification
Auto-selects the 5 highest-confidence SubConcepts from the uploaded lecture. Shows a generation spec with defaults (Bloom level 2-3, NBME format, 5 items). One big "Generate 5 questions — ~$0.60" button. Processing takes 60-90 seconds. This is intentionally fast and low-friction — the goal is for faculty to see actual questions from their lecture content before leaving the onboarding flow.
7
Review first questions — celebrate, then go to dashboard
Shows the 5 generated questions in a compact card list. Simple approve/reject per question. Copy: "These 5 questions came from your lecture. Approve any you like — they'll be added to your item bank." Completion screen shows items added count and takes faculty directly to their course dashboard with a tooltip tour of key features.

IV / Documents Tab

The faculty's personal document library — Google Drive meets medical knowledge graph

This Week view — the intelligence layer

What makes This Week special

This Week isn't a calendar. It's a briefing. For each teaching session this week, it shows: what lecture content maps to it, which USMLE topics are covered by that content, the LOD-enriched facts from the knowledge graph (drug mechanisms, disease associations, pathway links), how many assessment items are ready for those topics, and what gaps exist. It answers "am I prepared to assess what I'm teaching this week?" in a single view.

Linked knowledge — LOD enrichment
Furosemide (loop diuretic) — inhibits Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter in thick ascending limb. Hetionet: treats Heart Failure (strength 0.82), causes Hypokalemia, causes Ototoxicity.
BNP — released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stress. Clinical threshold: >100 pg/mL for HF diagnosis (sensitivity 90%, specificity 76%).
NYHA Class II → comfortable at rest, slight limitation with ordinary activity. Maps to USMLE topic: "Clinical features of CHF" under Cardiovascular system.

Tab 2 — Syllabus weeks

Full week-by-week view of the course. Each week expands to show: session names (from syllabus), associated lecture documents, extracted USMLE topics, item count per topic, and coverage percentage. Faculty can click any session to jump to its concepts, generate questions for that session, or see the pre-flight checklist. Dragging weeks reorders them. Adding a session creates a blank slot that can be associated with a lecture.

Tab 3 — Questions

All items associated with this course, with rich filtering: by USMLE system, Bloom level, QA score, status (approved/pending/rejected), week, generation session, or search by keyword. Bulk actions: approve all, export selected, add to collection, create exam from selection. Each item shows a stem preview, Bloom badge, USMLE system badge, QA score, and approval status. Click to open the full item with Toulmin chain and distractor rationale.

Tab 4 — Coverage

The USMLE coverage heatmap scoped to this specific course. 18 systems × 6 Bloom levels. Three states: gap (red), partial (amber), confirmed (green). Click any cell to see the SubConcepts in that cell, generate items for that gap, or view existing items. Header row shows overall system percentages. Side column shows Bloom level distribution. Quick filter: "Show gaps only" collapses to only red/amber cells.

Tab 5 — Assessments

All exams created for this course. Cards show: exam name, date, student count, average score, KR-20 reliability, item count, and status (draft/deployed/completed/archived). Click to open the assessment detail view with full item-by-item statistics. Actions: create new exam, duplicate, export to QTI, archive. Completed exams show: p-value distribution chart, discrimination index summary, and any flagged low-quality items.

Tab 6 — Students (course view)

All students enrolled in this course (across sections). Table view: name, section, assessments taken, average score, USMLE Step 1 estimated coverage based on their question responses, last active date. Click student to go to their full profile. Sort by: name, section, score, coverage, last active. Filter by section.

VII / Generation

Three modes — Quick Generate, Topic Spotlight (NLP form spike), and Blueprint

Mode 1 — Quick Generate (from course context)

Available from course dashboard, This Week view, or the Items tab. A right-side drawer slides in showing: selected course/week (pre-filled from context), top 5 SubConcepts sorted by coverage gap, Bloom level defaults, item count per concept. One-click generate. Shows cost estimate before triggering. Target: under 10 seconds from decision to generation started.

Mode 2 — Topic Spotlight (NLP form spike)

The design innovation

Topic Spotlight is the novel UX in Journey OS. Instead of navigating menus to specify what you want to generate, you interact directly with your lecture content. Terms that MetaMap/UMLS has recognized get a subtle underline. Click any underlined term and a smart dropdown shows the matched UMLS concept, its USMLE system, related LOD data, and a one-click "add to generation targets." The result feels like annotating your own slides — natural, fast, and medically precise. This is the generation flow that will make faculty say "I've never seen anything like this."

generate — topic spotlight
Lecture content — click any underlined term to add as generation target

Heart failure represents a complex clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet the body's metabolic demands. The hallmark of systolic heart failure (HFrEF) is a reduced ejection fraction below 40%, while HFpEF presents with preserved ejection fraction but impaired diastolic function.

The neurohormonal response activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous system, leading to sodium retention, vasoconstriction, and ventricular remodeling. This maladaptive response initially compensatory becomes detrimental over time.

First-line treatment includes ACE inhibitors or ARBs for afterload reduction, beta-blockers for rate control and reverse remodeling, and loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for symptom relief through volume reduction.

Mode 3 — Blueprint Generator (structured by USMLE system + Bloom)

For faculty who want precise control over coverage distribution. Select USMLE system, Bloom level distribution (slider bars for each level), item count, and topic depth. The system shows a coverage preview (what percentage of Step 1 topics will be covered if generated). Output is a structured batch generation — suitable for creating an entire exam's worth of items from a specified topic domain. Best for: department chairs building a comprehensive item bank, or faculty preparing for a high-stakes summative exam.

Assessment detail view — completed exam quality panel

Each completed assessment shows a full psychometric breakdown: score distribution histogram, KR-20 reliability coefficient (with target ≥0.70 flagged), item-by-item p-values and discrimination indices, any items flagged as low quality (p < 0.20 or discrimination < 0.20), and a comparison of this exam's results against the item bank's expected difficulty. Flagged low-quality items link back to the source lecture chunk — helping faculty understand whether the item was poor or whether the lecture content was unclear.

Assessment creation flow

Three entry paths: (1) Blueprint-first (specify USMLE system distribution, Bloom distribution, item count → system assembles from bank), (2) Topic-first (select specific concepts/weeks → system fills blueprint), (3) Manual assembly (search item bank and hand-pick). All three paths produce a blueprint preview showing coverage gaps before finalizing. The proximity constraint (no two items from the same SubConcept within 3 consecutive positions) is enforced automatically.

Four views — coverage, student performance, item quality, generation efficiency

Analytics sub-tabs

Sub-tabWhat it showsKey charts/viewsPrimary insight
CoverageUSMLE topic coverage across the institution and by course18-system heatmap (institution-wide), coverage over time trend, gaps vs. total topics by system"Your institution covers 74% of Step 1 Cardiovascular — Renal is 28%"

GenerationItem production efficiency and usageItems generated over time, approval rate trend, cost per item, items used in exams vs. never used"82% of generated items approved · avg $0.11/item · 34% of bank never used in exam"

Coverage analytics — the institution view

The institution-level heatmap shows aggregate coverage across all courses taught by this faculty member. Each cell in the 18×6 grid shows total items available for that system/Bloom combination. Mouse hover shows: item count, avg QA score, avg p-value from student responses. Click any red cell to jump directly to the gap-fill generation flow with that system/Bloom pre-selected. A "coverage report" export generates a one-page PDF suitable for LCME DCI submission.

Item quality analytics — flagged items panel

Items with p-value <0.20 (too hard) or >0.80 (too easy), discrimination index <0.20, or QA score <0.65 appear in the flagged items list. Each flagged item shows: why it was flagged, which student cohort it was tested on, the source lecture chunk, and one-click actions: regenerate (creates a replacement with the same topic/Bloom), edit, or archive. Running this analysis after every exam improves the item bank over time.

What "Remix" does
Remix opens the generation session with its original topics, Bloom levels, and context pre-loaded. You can change the clinical scenario angle, swap Bloom levels, increase item count, or change the distractor strategy — then re-run to generate a new set from the same source material. Useful for: creating harder versions of existing questions, generating more items when you've used up the approved ones, or trying a different clinical presentation angle.
